rationale: B wins because it finds the story Instacart would rather not lead with: "The checkout line is disappearing in a few hundred grocery stores. What happens to the people who staffed it?" That is the sharper editor-facing move than A's softer strategic wrapper, "Why 1,500 grocery banners are renting their tech stack instead of building it," which is useful but partly inferred. Both sets are strong; B just has a better nose for the hostile read and a cleaner next step.
gaps_in_A: "Instacart's delivery growth has stalled" overstates the fact. The update says growth slowed to single digits, not stalled.
"Why 1,500 grocery banners are renting their tech stack instead of building it" smuggles in a make-versus-buy decision the update does not prove.
"slowing core, accelerating adjacency" implies acceleration in the ad business. The update gives a $1B run rate, not growth rate.
The next step is too diffuse: "four viable shapes exist" is true, but the founder needs a first pitch priority, not a menu.
gaps_in_B: "a company that does not own a store" is likely true in the real world, but it is not in the supplied update. In this exercise, that is an invented support beam.
"ad business just passed $1 billion" is imprecise. The fact is a $1B annual run rate, not necessarily $1B recognized revenue.
"The count of advertisers is the hook" is good, but the angle still needs one named brand or format proof before it can carry a real trade pitch.
"This one looks at what the company is becoming and whether the market has noticed" is a little grand. Keep the investor question, lose the TED-talk fog.
